question: In traumatic hyphema, the most dangerous complication is secondary haemorrhage (rebleed), which typically occurs 3 to 5 days after the initial injury when the organising clot undergoes fibrinolysis and the ruptured vessel bleeds again.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is TRUE. Secondary haemorrhage (rebleed) in hyphema occurs at day 3–5 due to fibrinolysis of the primary clot — the vessel re-opens before it has healed. It carries a worse prognosis than the primary bleed. Management principles include rest, eye shielding, avoiding NSAIDs, and sometimes antifibrinolytics (tranexamic acid) to reduce rebleed risk.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. Secondary haemorrhage in hyphema classically occurs on day 3–5 as the primary clot undergoes fibrinolysis, exposing the still-fragile ruptured vessel. This rebleed is typically larger than the primary bleed, dramatically increases the risk of corneal blood staining, ghost cell glaucoma, and permanent visual loss. This is why patients with hyphema are admitted, rested, and monitored closely for 5 days.
